summary: Describes the Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP), which measures one-way and round-trip performance metrics such as delay, delay variation and packet loss by sending test packets between two endpoints.

plainLanguage.summary: You toss a ball to a friend and time how long it takes to come back. STAMP does that with test messages to see how fast and reliable a network path is.

questions: how to measure delay and packet loss with twamp-light
what udp port does stamp use
subtitle: A simple, interoperable way to send test packets between two endpoints and measure delay, delay variation and loss.

tldr.problem: TWAMP Light implementations were hard to make interoperate because RFC 5357 did not specify them well enough, and operators wanted a simpler test protocol with test and control kept separate.
tldr.mechanism: A Session-Sender sends UDP test packets with a sequence number and timestamp to a Session-Reflector, which sends back a reply carrying its own receive and transmit timestamps. The packets can be unauthenticated or protected with an HMAC.
tldr.outcome: STAMP measures one-way and round-trip delay, delay variation and packet loss, and unauthenticated mode interworks with TWAMP Light. It is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated by RFC 8972.

today: RFC 8762 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8972; it has not been obsoleted. The RFC itself describes STAMP as intended for production networks.

sections.title: Why STAMP Exists
sections.content:
The Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP, RFC 5357) and its extensions gave operators useful experience, and several independent implementations of TWAMP and TWAMP Light have been deployed. At the same time there was interest in a more straightforward mechanism that behaves deterministically and keeps the test function separate from control, which is vendor-specific configuration or orchestration.

The RFC points out that work by the Broadband Forum showed interoperability among TWAMP Light implementations is difficult, because RFC 5357 did not specify TWAMP Light sufficiently. STAMP, the Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol, is the answer: an active test protocol that measures both one-way and round-trip performance metrics, such as delay, delay variation and packet loss.
sections.plainLanguage: Different companies built their own versions of a network speed-test and they did not always work together. STAMP is a simpler, clearer version everyone can follow.

sections.title: Sender, Reflector and Sessions
sections.content:
A STAMP session is the two-way packet flow between one Session-Sender and one Session-Reflector for some period of time. How sessions and endpoints are configured and managed is out of scope; the RFC lists a command line interface, OSS/BSS systems, SNMP and NETCONF/YANG controllers as examples.

The Session-Sender sends test packets over UDP to the Session-Reflector. The sender MUST use UDP port 862 as the default destination port, and it must also be able to use ports from the User Ports and Dynamic Ports ranges. The reflector MUST listen on port 862 by default and be able to use other ports from those ranges. By default the packets are symmetrical: the reply is the same size as the request.

The reflector works in one of two modes. In stateless mode it keeps no test state and copies the received sequence number, so only round-trip loss can be calculated. In stateful mode it keeps state for each session and numbers its replies itself, which lets the sender tell forward loss from backward loss.
sections.plainLanguage: One kid throws numbered balls and another throws them back. If the thrower keeps a tally, they can tell whether the balls got lost on the way there or on the way back.

sections.title: The Session-Sender Test Packet
sections.content:
The base sender packet is 44 octets in unauthenticated mode and 112 octets in authenticated mode. It carries a 4-octet Sequence Number that starts at zero for each new session and goes up by one per packet, an 8-octet Timestamp, and a 2-octet Error Estimate. The rest is Must-Be-Zero (MBZ) padding, which makes the sender packet match the size of the larger reflected packet.

Nodes MUST support the NTP version 4 64-bit timestamp format and MAY support the IEEE 1588v2 PTP truncated 64-bit format. The Z bit in the Error Estimate says which one is in use: 0 for NTP, 1 for PTPv2. NTP is the default. MBZ fields MUST be zero when sent and ignored on receipt.

In authenticated mode the packet is padded with MBZ fields to a multiple of 16 octets and ends with a 16-octet HMAC.
sections.plainLanguage: Each test packet is a numbered postcard with the exact time written on it, plus some blank space so the reply can be the same size.

sections.title: The Session-Reflector Reply
sections.content:
If the reflector validates the base test packet, it sends back a reply of symmetrical size, copying any content beyond the base packet. The reply carries its own Sequence Number, Timestamp (taken at the start of transmitting) and Receive Timestamp (when the test packet arrived), plus copies of the sender's sequence number, timestamp and error estimate.

It also includes a 1-octet Session-Sender TTL field, which is a copy of the TTL (IPv4) or Hop Limit (IPv6) of the received packet. The other bytes are MBZ fields that keep fields aligned on four-octet boundaries. As with the sender, authenticated mode adds more MBZ padding and a 16-octet HMAC at the end.
sections.plainLanguage: The friend writes back on the same postcard: when it arrived, when it was sent back, and a copy of what you wrote, so you can do the math.

sections.title: Integrity and Confidentiality
sections.content:
Authenticated mode protects each STAMP message with an HMAC. STAMP uses HMAC-SHA-256 truncated to 128 bits, so the HMAC field is 16 octets. It covers the first six blocks (96 octets) of the packet, and it MUST be verified as early as possible so corrupted data is not used or passed on.

The HMAC uses its own key, which may differ for each test session. Key management and key distribution are outside the scope of the RFC; it suggests an orchestrator configuring the key through the STAMP YANG data model as one example. Future specifications may define stronger algorithms.

STAMP itself does not encrypt anything. If confidentiality is required, a session MUST use a secured transport, for example an IPsec tunnel or Datagram Transport Layer Security.
sections.plainLanguage: A secret stamp on each postcard shows nobody changed it on the way. If you want nobody to read it, you put it in a locked box.

sections.title: Working With TWAMP Light
sections.content:
Interworking with TWAMP Light devices was an essential requirement. Because STAMP uses HMAC-SHA-256 in authenticated mode while TWAMP uses HMAC-SHA-1, interoperability is considered only for unauthenticated mode. Two combinations are possible: a STAMP sender with a TWAMP Light reflector, and a TWAMP Light sender with a STAMP reflector.

A TWAMP Light reflector may not support port 862, so a STAMP sender may use another port. Any STAMP extensions are seen by TWAMP Light as the Packet Padding field. When the sender is TWAMP Light and cannot use port 862, the test management system MUST set the STAMP reflector to another permitted port and to the default NTP timestamp format.

A STAMP reflector answers a packet smaller than the base packet with the base reply, and answers a larger one by copying the extra content to keep the sizes symmetrical.
sections.plainLanguage: STAMP can play catch with the older game's players, as long as nobody uses the secret stamp, since the two games stamp differently.

sections.title: Operational and Security Considerations
sections.content:
STAMP is meant for production networks, so operators can assess service level agreements based on delay, delay variation and loss. The load of test packets MUST be carefully estimated and its impact on existing services thoroughly analyzed. When using the Internet, especially with User Ports, the use MUST be agreed by the users of the nodes hosting the sender and reflector before a session starts. Guidance on UDP load comes from RFC 8085.

Security considerations come from OWAMP-Test (RFC 4656) and from the use of the well-known port, covered in RFC 8545. Because configuration and management are out of scope, the RFC sets one general rule: control and management of a STAMP session MUST use secured transport. HMAC-SHA-256 in authenticated mode protects the integrity of test packets. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Test packets use up some of the road, so you have to ask the road's owners first and not send too many.

messages.label: Test packet

messages.label: Reflected packet
messages.note: Adds receive timestamp and its own timestamp; copies the sender's fields.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Starts at zero for a new session, plus one per packet.

fields.name: Timestamp
fields.desc: NTP 64-bit format by default; PTP truncated format optional.

fields.name: Error Estimate
fields.desc: S, Z, Scale and Multiplier; Z says NTP (0) or PTPv2 (1).

fields.name: MBZ
fields.desc: 30 octets, zero on send and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Copied from the sender (stateless) or counted by the reflector (stateful).

fields.name: Timestamp
fields.desc: Taken by the reflector at the start of transmitting.

fields.name: Error Estimate
fields.desc: Same size and meaning as in the sender packet.

fields.name: MBZ
fields.desc: Zero on send, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Receive Timestamp
fields.desc: When the test packet arrived at the reflector.

fields.name: Session-Sender Sequence Number
fields.desc: Copy of the sender's sequence number.

fields.name: Session-Sender Error Estimate
fields.desc: Copy of the sender's error estimate.

fields.name: MBZ
fields.desc: Zero on send, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Session-Sender TTL
fields.desc: Copy of the TTL or Hop Limit of the received packet.

fields.desc: Zero on send, ignored on receipt.
